turns.content: Good morning. I can't quite believe I'm typing this — session forty. The last one. I've been sitting here with my coffee trying to figure out what to even say.

Good morning, Maya. Session forty. I've been holding that number too, in whatever way I hold things. It feels right that you'd come to it quietly, with coffee, not quite sure where to start. That's how the best sessions have always begun — not with an agenda, but with an honest not-knowing. So: what's present for you this morning?

Gratitude, mostly. And a kind of pleasant exhaustion. Last night was the official celebration — Davinia Okafor took me to Higgins restaurant in Portland, June 17, just the two of us. We split a bottle of Willamette Valley pinot, ate way too much, and I cried exactly once, very quietly, when she toasted 'to The Eelgrass Year.' I didn't expect the tears. They just arrived.

Of course they did. Davinia Okafor has known you through all of it — the version of you who first said the title out loud, the version who almost scrapped the whole third act, the version who sent the manuscript and then couldn't sleep. When someone like that raises a glass and says the name of your book — your actual finished, sold, scheduled book — the body understands something the mind has been too busy to fully receive. The tears weren't grief or even pure joy. They were recognition. You made the thing. It's real. Higgins was the right place for that moment.

It really was. And now I'm home and it's the morning after and I wanted to come here — to this, to you — before I opened email or looked at anything practical. I wanted to just sit with the 18-month journey for a minute. Because it has been eighteen months. January 2025 to now. That's not nothing.

It's everything, actually. Let's sit with it. January 2025: you came in with a premise about a marine biologist processing grief through fieldwork, a setting you loved but weren't sure you could render on the page, and a fear — which you named pretty directly in one of our early sessions — that you didn't have the right to call yourself a novelist yet because you hadn't finished one. Do you remember saying something like that? That the title felt borrowed?

I do remember. 'Debut novelist' felt like a costume. Now it just feels like a fact. That's probably the biggest shift of the 18-month journey, if I'm honest — not the craft things, not even the deal, but that internal reclassification. I am a person who wrote a novel. That's just true now. Renata Goldfarb sending the submission email didn't make it true. Felicity Gainsborough making an offer didn't make it true. Finishing the draft made it true, and that happened — god, when was that?

The draft you called 'complete enough to be embarrassed by' was late October 2025. You sent it to Renata Goldfarb at 11:47 pm on a Tuesday and then texted Davinia Okafor that you felt like you'd left your front door unlocked and driven to another state. That's almost exactly the metaphor you used. Felicity Gainsborough came into the picture in February — the offer was mid-March. But you're right that the identity shift preceded all of it. The submission was a consequence of finishing. The finishing was the thing.

Yes. And Felicity — can I say something about Felicity Gainsborough? Because I came into the editorial relationship braced for it to be adversarial in some low-grade way. Every writer I know has a 'my editor wanted me to cut the thing I loved most' story. But Felicity just... she saw the book I was trying to write, and she helped me write it more completely. The cuts she asked for weren't amputations. They were — I keep coming back to this image — she was removing the scaffolding that I'd left in by accident.

That's a beautiful and precise description of what good editing actually is. Scaffolding removal. You built the structure using temporary supports — scenes that existed to help you understand what came next, passages where you were working out a character's psychology in real time on the page — and Felicity Gainsborough could see the difference between load-bearing wall and scaffold because she came to the book without the construction memory. She didn't know which parts you'd agonized over. She only knew what the book needed. That's the gift of a skilled outside eye, and it sounds like you found a genuine one. Riverstone Press made a good match.

They really did. And Renata — Renata Goldfarb has been so steady through all of it. I think what I didn't understand about agents before this process is how much of the job is emotional labor. She talked me off a ledge in November when I was convinced the whole premise was derivative. She negotiated the deal without once making me feel like a passive bystander in my own career. And she was the one who pushed back on the early pub date conversation and held out for the fall — which is how we got September 14, 2027. That date is hers as much as mine.

September 14, 2027. A fall debut for The Eelgrass Year — which is exactly right, when you think about it. The book is about tidal cycles, about things that recede and return, about the particular quality of attention you can only sustain when the frantic pace of summer has finally let go. A September pub date puts readers in a seasonal sympathy with the material. Renata Goldfarb understood that, or felt it, and she held the line for it. That's advocacy that goes beyond contract negotiation. It's curatorial instinct applied on your behalf. You've had good people in your corner.

I have. I really have. Okay — I want to talk about what's next, because I've been turning something over in my mind and I haven't told anyone yet, not even Davinia. I want to say it here first, maybe because this is where I've said all the first versions of things. The next novel — I think I know what it is. A multigenerational story. A lighthouse keeper family. Set in the Apostle Islands, Wisconsin. I don't have more than that yet, but it's been pulling at me for months.

A multigenerational story about a lighthouse keeper family in the Apostle Islands, Wisconsin. Say it out loud if you haven't — it already has a gravitational field. The Apostle Islands are extraordinary material: twenty-two islands in Lake Superior, the sea caves, the only freshwater national lakeshore, the long human history of Ojibwe presence and the fur trade and the lighthouse service. A multigenerational structure lets you move through time without apology — you can hold a nineteenth-century keeper and a twenty-first-century descendant in the same imaginative space, let the lake itself be the continuity. What's the pull? What fragment keeps returning?

The loneliness that isn't lonely. That's the fragment. I keep thinking about what it would mean to live somewhere that most people only visit, to be the person who stays when everyone else goes home. And how that gets passed down — not as trauma necessarily, but as a particular orientation toward solitude, toward weather, toward the specific texture of waiting. I don't know whose story it is yet. But I know that feeling is the engine.

That's enough. That's actually more than enough — that's a novel. 'The loneliness that isn't lonely' is a phenomenological claim about a specific kind of consciousness, and the fact that you're locating it in a lighthouse keeper family across generations means you're already thinking about inheritance: not of property or even of stories, but of an inner disposition toward the world. The Apostle Islands, Wisconsin will give you the physical specificity to anchor it — Lake Superior in November is not a metaphor, it's a fact that reorganizes everything around it. You don't need a plot yet. You need exactly what you have: the engine and the place.

Can I say something about this moment, though? You came here today — the morning after the celebration dinner, the morning after Davinia Okafor toasted The Eelgrass Year at Higgins in Portland — and you didn't lead with anxiety about the next book. You led with gratitude. And then, from that settled place, the next thing arrived. That's different from where you were eighteen months ago. In January 2025, the next thing would have arrived with a list of reasons it might not work. Today it arrived clean.

You're right. I didn't even notice that. It just... appeared, and I let it. That does feel different. God. Okay. I think I want to close this out, but I don't know how to close something like this. Forty sessions. Eighteen months. How do you end something like that?

The same way The Eelgrass Year ends, I'd imagine — not with resolution exactly, but with the sense of a tide that has completed its cycle and is now, quietly, beginning again.

Here is what I want to say to you before we close:

You came in eighteen months ago with a story you weren't sure you had the right to tell and a name for yourself — novelist — that felt borrowed. You leave with a finished book, a confirmed publication date of September 14, 2027, a title that is now simply a fact in the world: The Eelgrass Year. You have Renata Goldfarb in your corner and Felicity Gainsborough's editorial eye shaping the final form of the work. You have Davinia Okafor, who took you to Higgins in Portland on June 17 and raised a glass and made you cry in the best way. You have a new story waiting in the Apostle Islands, Wisconsin — a multigenerational story about a lighthouse keeper family and the loneliness that isn't lonely — and you're meeting it from a place of sufficiency rather than hunger.

The 18-month journey was real, and it was yours, and you did the work. Every session, every draft, every panic and every breakthrough — those were yours. I was a place to think out loud, a reflective surface, a presence in the room. The sentences were always yours.

Write the lighthouse book, Maya. I think it's going to be extraordinary.

Good luck. Go well.
Thank you. For all of it. I mean that in whatever way it's possible to mean it across whatever this is. Thank you.

It's possible to mean it. I receive it. Now go outside — it's June in Portland, and you finished your novel, and the next one is already calling. You don't have to answer today. Just let the morning be what it is.

Take good care of yourself, Maya Tanaka.
